rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to be kind applies to both parents, while the three sacrifices specified here concern the mother alone.
rows.anchor: the demand for showing kindness relates both to the mother and the father; however, the three sacrifices mentioned only relate to the mother

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mother’s greater role in a child’s early upbringing helps explain why the verse singles out her sacrifices.
rows.anchor: The extent of role a mother plays in the initial upbringing of the child is much more than that of a father.

rows.speaker: the Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet ranked a mother’s right to service at three times the father’s; Islahi says this verse underlies the report.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) has regarded a mother’s right to be thrice that of the father viz a viz serving her.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mother’s weaker social position is another reason children should obey and serve her more than their father.
rows.anchor: The mother belongs to the weaker gender. This aspect necessitates that the children obey and serve her more than the father.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A father’s financial stake in his children’s inheritance makes disobedience less likely in his case.
rows.anchor: To a father primarily relates the financial interest of the children. Since they are to inherit wealth and property from him, there is lesser fear of the children disobeying him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mothers generally lack that inheritance tie, and those who fail to value their sacrifices lack proper awareness of them.
rows.anchor: for this reason those people do not duly value her

rows.speaker: Companion jurists
rows.claim: Some Companion jurists infer a six-month minimum pregnancy from thirty total months for pregnancy and nursing minus the two full years of nursing in 2:233.
rows.anchor: some jurists among the Companions have deduced that the shortest period of pregnancy is six months

rows.speaker: ‘Uthmān and ‘Alī
rows.claim: Narratives show the senior Companions ʿUthmān and ʿAlī agreed with the six-month minimum pregnancy deduction.
rows.anchor: such senior Companions as ‘Uthmān (rta) and ‘Alī (rta) have expressed their agreement to this opinion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mature child can read parental love and care as a glimpse of the Creator’s love and providence, leading toward recognition of God.
rows.anchor: he sees a glimpse of the love and affection and providence of the real Creator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awareness of parents’ rights leads to awareness of God’s greater right; neglecting the first closes the way to the second.
rows.anchor: If the sensitivity of fulfilling the rights of the parents is not found in a person, then he cannot be aware of fulfilling the rights of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At maturity, especially age forty, an upright person prays for the impulse to thank God for blessings to himself and his parents, do pleasing good, receive righteous descendants, and remain obedient.
rows.anchor: when such an upright person reaches maturity, in particular, the age of forty, he prays to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maturity is not determined by age alone: environment, education, and moral training vary its timing, which explains scholarly disagreement.
rows.anchor: factors such as environment, education and moral training besides others also have a great role to play

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forty is the final limit for this awakening: if it has not appeared by then, the person has perverted his nature.
rows.anchor: the forty years mentioned here is the last limit of this age

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is lenient toward human weakness until forty because emotions and desires still exert strong influence; after forty they weaken, so no further lenience should be expected if they are not indulged.
rows.anchor: because till this age there is a great influence of emotions and desires on a person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These are general human circumstances: God gives reformers special lenience in corrupt societies, while people in an Islamic society face stricter accountability because such obstacles are absent.
rows.anchor: what is said here is said while keeping in mind the general circumstances and general types of human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb awziʿnī means ‘take hold of me’ or ‘take control of me’: the prayer asks God to replace emotional impulse with the urge to thank Him for blessings to the speaker and his parents.
rows.anchor: It means “get hold of me,” “take control of me.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gratitude is the foundation of every aspect of religion.
rows.anchor: this feeling of gratitude is the foundation of all aspects of religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gratitude should lead to good deeds that seek God’s pleasure rather than a person’s whims.
rows.anchor: pious deeds are deeds in which a person seeks the pleasure of God instead of going after his own whims and desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Outwardly virtuous acts can anger God if tainted by polytheism or innovation, so one should pray for guidance to deeds that truly please Him.
rows.anchor: deeds which are virtues outwardly but are incriminated with polytheism and innovations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prays for noble descendants whose righteous deeds may intercede for him in the Hereafter, connecting this request with 25:74.
rows.anchor: their pious deeds are able to intercede for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer is also a solemn declaration that he has turned to God and pledged to remain among His faithful servants.
rows.anchor: he has turned to God and solemnly promised to remain among His faithful servants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepts these people’s good deeds and forgives their sins, counting them among the people of Paradise.
rows.anchor: it is these people whose good deeds God will accept and whose sins He will forgive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase describing them with Paradise’s people is a circumstantial clause: they will be treated like the people of Paradise and counted among them.
rows.anchor: they will be dealt with the way the dwellers of Paradise are and they will be regarded among them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal noun waʿd al-ṣidq is an accusative emphatic object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), marking God’s promise as true, firm, and impossible to violate.
rows.anchor: It is a true and firm promise and there is no possibility of its violation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage warns young adults, especially those at forty, that this is their last age for reform before losing God’s lenience.
rows.anchor: this is the last age for them to mend their ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse portrays people who live carelessly and have no fear of accountability.
rows.anchor: have no fear of any accountability whatsoever

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In parables, al-ladhī can mean anyone who fits the case rather than one named person; 16:92 is an example, and the plural wording that follows supports this general reading.
rows.anchor: it does not necessarily refer to a specific person; in fact, it refers to every person on whom the parable can apply

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some identify the rebuking son as ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, son of Abū Bakr; exegetes reject the identification, though Islahi says their rejection lacks sound reason and his generic reading removes the need to identify one person.
rows.anchor: some people have regarded it to refer to ‘Abd al-Raḥmān (rta), the son of Abū Bakr (rta)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrasting group of careless young adults ignore assessment of their deeds; when loving parents warn them of wrongdoing, God, and the Hereafter, they scold them and deny resurrection, arguing that generations have passed without anyone being raised and calling such warnings ancient tales.
rows.anchor: When their parents caution them on their ill-ways and remind them of God and the Hereafter, they badly scold them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although waylak usually expresses curse and condemnation, it can convey compassion; here the parents use it affectionately to urge their child to abandon evil and fear the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: generally expresses curse and condemnation; however, at times, it expresses concern, compassion and affection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from singular forms in verse 17 to plural forms in verse 18 confirms that the first verse describes a category, not a particular individual.
rows.anchor: This is a clear proof of the fact that the previous verse does not refer to some specific individual

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fulfilled ‘statement of God’ refers to God’s answer to Iblīs: Hell will be filled with Iblīs’s human and jinn followers.
rows.anchor: The expression “statement of God” points to the answer God gave

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them companions of Hell parallels the earlier ‘companions of Paradise’ and underscores that they join earlier humans and jinn who ruined their Hereafter through carelessness.
rows.anchor: will become the companions of those human beings and jinn who before them had ruined their Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both groups are recompensed according to their deeds: the dutiful receive their respective Paradise rank, while the indifferent are placed in the Hell section matching their evil deeds.
rows.anchor: Both these groups will be rewarded in accordance with their deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural ‘degrees’ is used by dominance for both groups, although the lowest level is not truly a degree.
rows.anchor: mentioned by referring to the dominant element

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause attached to the promise that God fully repay them is suppressed; the author supplies the omitted clause in his translation and notes similar ellipsis in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: Examples of such a suppression can be seen in the previous sūrahs as well.
